   - Next best test: Provocative evaluation with fiberoptic laryngoscopy during symptomatic episode (or continuous observation) and inspiratory flow-volume loops.

   - Rationale: Dry cough, increased work of breathing without fever, normal upper-airway anatomy; lower-airway bronchospasm may not be seen on bronchoscopy.
   - Next best test: Auscultation for wheeze and trial of inhaled bronchodilator; spirometry/peak flow if tolerated.

3. Laryngeal sensory neuropathy / cough-hypersensitivity syndrome after airway instrumentation — 3rd
   - Rationale: Persistent dry cough beginning after surgical airway manipulation with normal anatomic exam; known cause of chronic cough after intubation/suctioning.
   - Next best test: Empiric therapeutic trial (neuromodulator or speech/laryngeal therapy) and ENT/voice therapy assessment; laryngopharyngeal reflux evaluation as adjunct.

4. Small-volume aspiration or aspiration bronchitis (chemical pneumonitis) — 4th
   - Rationale: Onset the day after surgery raises possibility of perioperative microaspiration; may present with cough and respiratory effort without gross endoscopic airway findings.
   - Next best test: Chest radiograph (or chest CT if x-ray equivocal) and clinical review for vomiting/regurgitation events; consider bronchoalveolar lavage only if infection suspected.

5. Intermittent postoperative laryngospasm / transient upper‑airway edema not captured on exam — Less likely
   - Rationale: History of stridor and respiratory difficulty early post-op could reflect transient events that resolved prior to scope; normal endoscopy makes persistent structural edema unlikely.
   - Next best test: Continuous bedside observation during symptomatic periods; consider short trial of systemic steroid and nebulized epinephrine if recurrent acute episodes.
